metadata.narrative: Propose a biologically plausible model that integrates the neuroscience concepts of engrams and predictive coding into one network capable of performing classification tasks.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A biologically plausible classifier can be built by fusing two well-established but previously separate neuroscience frameworks: the engram, the physical trace of a memory carried by a sparse population of neurons, and predictive coding, the theory that cortex continuously compares top-down predictions with bottom-up sensory evidence.

Call the resulting architecture a Predictive Engram Network, in which each hierarchical level of a canonical cortical microcircuit hosts a competitively allocated engram ensemble that simultaneously serves as a generative prior for predictive coding and as an attractor state for associative memory, and classification emerges as selecting which engram best explains sensory input with minimal residual error.

Engram cells are defined by allocation experiments as a sparse, competitively selected subset of eligible neurons, commonly under twenty to thirty percent of an eligible population in the lateral amygdala, that wins recruitment because of transiently elevated intrinsic excitability driven by the transcription factor CREB.

This excitability-based competition also governs how multiple engrams interact, producing overlapping or linked memories, silent engrams that are reactivatable but not spontaneously retrieved, and engram complexes distributed across brain regions.

At the cellular level, engrams are Hebbian assemblies: immediate-early gene expression such as Arc marks a stable population whose activity patterns and synaptic weights persist for weeks and are reactivated during recall.

Storage also depends on synapse-specific plasticity: a CaMKII-CREB-CBP signaling cascade drives plasticity-related-protein synthesis, while a transient, activity-dependent tag at a specific synapse captures those proteins to convert early into late long-term potentiation, a mechanism called synaptic tagging and capture.

Memory strength is carried not merely by isolated synaptic weights but by an engram-to-engram circuit spanning multiple regions, since optogenetic reactivation can restore recall in amnesic animals whose synapses were never potentiated.
Dual-labeling studies confirm that potentiation between engram cells in successive stages, such as hippocampal CA3 and CA1, scales with the behavioral strength of memory expression.

Predictive coding, in Rao and Ballard's formulation, treats sensory input as generated by hidden causes through a learned generative model, so perception becomes inference of the hidden state that best explains input, and learning becomes tuning the top-down synaptic matrix encoding that model.

Implementation requires two neuron types at every level except the top: prediction neurons carrying the current estimate of hidden causes, and error neurons computing the residual between top-down prediction and actual lower-level activity, sending that residual upward while predictions flow downward.

This exchange has an anatomical home in the canonical cortical microcircuit, where layer four receives feedforward input, layer two/three pyramidal cells carry feedforward error signals upward, and layer five/six pyramidal cells send feedback predictions downward, matching accounts of cortical message passing between hidden causes and hidden states.

A single pyramidal neuron can itself implement this comparison, since basal dendrites near the soma integrate bottom-up drive while distal apical dendrites integrate top-down feedback, generating calcium-dependent plateau potentials explicitly linked to the feedback/feedforward division predictive coding requires.

The two literatures already converge computationally: predictive-coding networks that settle prediction errors to equilibrium compute exactly the gradients backpropagation would compute, a result shown for multilayer perceptrons and generalized to arbitrary computation graphs, so a predictive-coding network can be trained toward a classification target using only locally available error signals.

The same predictive-coding architecture has already been shown capable of acting simultaneously as a classifier, a generative model, and an associative memory on arbitrary graph topologies, precisely the multifunctionality an engram-based classifier needs.
The proposed network exploits this convergence directly.

At each level, candidate units compete for allocation to that level's active representation exactly as amygdala neurons compete via CREB-driven excitability, so units with highest transient excitability become that level's engram for the current input.

Feedforward error neurons at each level, implemented as layer two/three pyramidal cells, compute the mismatch between sensory-driven basal-dendrite activity and the top-down apical-dendrite prediction generated by the engram ensemble one level up.

Top-level engram ensembles behave as fixed-point attractors: recurrent connectivity, following the sparse but structured connectivity found in hippocampal CA3, drives partial or noisy inputs toward the nearest stored pattern, implementing pattern completion.

Class output is read out the way CA1 reads CA3: only when the recurrent network converges into a coordinated burst representing a genuine attractor does the decision propagate downstream, so the winning class is whichever top-level engram both minimizes residual error and reaches a stable attractor fastest.
Learning combines two locally computable signals rather than global backpropagation.

Within-trial synaptic change follows a three-factor Hebbian rule in which pre- and post-synaptic firing set eligible synapses while a diffuse neuromodulatory signal proportional to classification error acts as the third factor, a scheme already shown to approach backpropagation-level image-classification accuracy using only biologically available quantities.

Consolidation into a durable engram synapse follows synaptic tagging and capture: synapses active during a large-error trial are tagged, and only a sufficiently strong neuromodulatory signal triggers protein synthesis to capture that tag, so unresolved large errors preferentially recruit new engram units rather than overwriting existing ones.

Because reactivation strength and behaviorally measured memory strength correlate in biological engrams, classification confidence can be read directly from the degree of engram reactivation rather than from an added readout layer.
This design yields falsifiable predictions.
It predicts that novel, high-error categories should recruit previously low-excitability, unallocated units rather than degrading existing class representations, mirroring competitive allocation.

It predicts that errors on ambiguous inputs should correspond to partial attractor convergence or silent engram-like states that are reactivatable but not spontaneously retrieved, paralleling silent engrams observed in amnesia research.

Remaining gaps include the absence of direct experimental tests of this exact combined circuit, uncertainty about how one neuromodulatory channel could carry class-specific teaching signals for many categories, and untested scalability of the sparse attractor-plus-predictive-coding scheme to deep hierarchies.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

A biologically plausible classifier can be built by fusing two well-established but previously separate neuroscience frameworks: the engram, the physical trace of a memory carried by a sparse population of neurons, and predictive coding, the theory that cortex continuously compares top-down predictions with bottom-up sensory evidence.
Call the resulting architecture a Predictive Engram Network, in which each hierarchical level of a canonical cortical microcircuit hosts a competitively allocated engram ensemble that simultaneously serves as a generative prior for predictive coding and as an attractor state for associative memory, and classification emerges as selecting which engram best explains sensory input with minimal residual error.

Engram cells are defined by allocation experiments as a sparse, competitively selected subset of eligible neurons, commonly under twenty to thirty percent of an eligible population in the lateral amygdala, that wins recruitment because of transiently elevated intrinsic excitability driven by the transcription factor CREB.

This excitability-based competition also governs how multiple engrams interact, producing overlapping or linked memories, silent engrams that are reactivatable but not spontaneously retrieved, and engram complexes distributed across brain regions.

At the cellular level, engrams are Hebbian assemblies: immediate-early gene expression such as Arc marks a stable population whose activity patterns and synaptic weights persist for weeks and are reactivated during recall.

[05901_46131]
Memory strength is carried not merely by isolated synaptic weights but by an engram-to-engram circuit spanning multiple regions, since optogenetic reactivation can restore recall in amnesic animals whose synapses were never potentiated.
[01162_40309]
Dual-labeling studies confirm that potentiation between engram cells in successive stages, such as hippocampal CA3 and CA1, scales with the behavioral strength of memory expression.
[01276_2163]

Predictive coding, in Rao and Ballard's formulation, treats sensory input as generated by hidden causes through a learned generative model, so perception becomes inference of the hidden state that best explains input, and learning becomes tuning the top-down synaptic matrix encoding that model.
[00586_75637]
Implementation requires two neuron types at every level except the top: prediction neurons carrying the current estimate of hidden causes, and error neurons computing the residual between top-down prediction and actual lower-level activity, sending that residual upward while predictions flow downward.
[01969_70115]
This exchange has an anatomical home in the canonical cortical microcircuit, where layer four receives feedforward input, layer two/three pyramidal cells carry feedforward error signals upward, and layer five/six pyramidal cells send feedback predictions downward, matching accounts of cortical message passing between hidden causes and hidden states.

This design yields falsifiable predictions.

[00445_65982] [05901_46131]
It predicts that errors on ambiguous inputs should correspond to partial attractor convergence or silent engram-like states that are reactivatable but not spontaneously retrieved, paralleling silent engrams observed in amnesia research.
[00445_65982] [01162_40309]
Remaining gaps include the absence of direct experimental tests of this exact combined circuit, uncertainty about how one neuromodulatory channel could carry class-specific teaching signals for many categories, and untested scalability of the sparse attractor-plus-predictive-coding scheme to deep hierarchies.

answer.text: A biologically plausible classifier can be built by fusing two well-established but previously separate neuroscience frameworks: the engram, the physical trace of a memory carried by a sparse population of neurons, and predictive coding, the theory that cortex continuously compares top-down predictions with bottom-up sensory evidence.

Call the resulting architecture a Predictive Engram Network, in which each hierarchical level of a canonical cortical microcircuit hosts a competitively allocated engram ensemble that simultaneously serves as a generative prior for predictive coding and as an attractor state for associative memory, and classification emerges as selecting which engram best explains sensory input with minimal residual error.

Engram cells are defined by allocation experiments as a sparse, competitively selected subset of eligible neurons, commonly under twenty to thirty percent of an eligible population in the lateral amygdala, that wins recruitment because of transiently elevated intrinsic excitability driven by the transcription factor CREB.

This excitability-based competition also governs how multiple engrams interact, producing overlapping or linked memories, silent engrams that are reactivatable but not spontaneously retrieved, and engram complexes distributed across brain regions.

At the cellular level, engrams are Hebbian assemblies: immediate-early gene expression such as Arc marks a stable population whose activity patterns and synaptic weights persist for weeks and are reactivated during recall.

Storage also depends on synapse-specific plasticity: a CaMKII-CREB-CBP signaling cascade drives plasticity-related-protein synthesis, while a transient, activity-dependent tag at a specific synapse captures those proteins to convert early into late long-term potentiation, a mechanism called synaptic tagging and capture.

Memory strength is carried not merely by isolated synaptic weights but by an engram-to-engram circuit spanning multiple regions, since optogenetic reactivation can restore recall in amnesic animals whose synapses were never potentiated.
Dual-labeling studies confirm that potentiation between engram cells in successive stages, such as hippocampal CA3 and CA1, scales with the behavioral strength of memory expression.

Predictive coding, in Rao and Ballard's formulation, treats sensory input as generated by hidden causes through a learned generative model, so perception becomes inference of the hidden state that best explains input, and learning becomes tuning the top-down synaptic matrix encoding that model.

Implementation requires two neuron types at every level except the top: prediction neurons carrying the current estimate of hidden causes, and error neurons computing the residual between top-down prediction and actual lower-level activity, sending that residual upward while predictions flow downward.

This exchange has an anatomical home in the canonical cortical microcircuit, where layer four receives feedforward input, layer two/three pyramidal cells carry feedforward error signals upward, and layer five/six pyramidal cells send feedback predictions downward, matching accounts of cortical message passing between hidden causes and hidden states.

A single pyramidal neuron can itself implement this comparison, since basal dendrites near the soma integrate bottom-up drive while distal apical dendrites integrate top-down feedback, generating calcium-dependent plateau potentials explicitly linked to the feedback/feedforward division predictive coding requires.

The two literatures already converge computationally: predictive-coding networks that settle prediction errors to equilibrium compute exactly the gradients backpropagation would compute, a result shown for multilayer perceptrons and generalized to arbitrary computation graphs, so a predictive-coding network can be trained toward a classification target using only locally available error signals.

The same predictive-coding architecture has already been shown capable of acting simultaneously as a classifier, a generative model, and an associative memory on arbitrary graph topologies, precisely the multifunctionality an engram-based classifier needs.
The proposed network exploits this convergence directly.

At each level, candidate units compete for allocation to that level's active representation exactly as amygdala neurons compete via CREB-driven excitability, so units with highest transient excitability become that level's engram for the current input.

Feedforward error neurons at each level, implemented as layer two/three pyramidal cells, compute the mismatch between sensory-driven basal-dendrite activity and the top-down apical-dendrite prediction generated by the engram ensemble one level up.

Top-level engram ensembles behave as fixed-point attractors: recurrent connectivity, following the sparse but structured connectivity found in hippocampal CA3, drives partial or noisy inputs toward the nearest stored pattern, implementing pattern completion.

Class output is read out the way CA1 reads CA3: only when the recurrent network converges into a coordinated burst representing a genuine attractor does the decision propagate downstream, so the winning class is whichever top-level engram both minimizes residual error and reaches a stable attractor fastest.
Learning combines two locally computable signals rather than global backpropagation.

Within-trial synaptic change follows a three-factor Hebbian rule in which pre- and post-synaptic firing set eligible synapses while a diffuse neuromodulatory signal proportional to classification error acts as the third factor, a scheme already shown to approach backpropagation-level image-classification accuracy using only biologically available quantities.

Consolidation into a durable engram synapse follows synaptic tagging and capture: synapses active during a large-error trial are tagged, and only a sufficiently strong neuromodulatory signal triggers protein synthesis to capture that tag, so unresolved large errors preferentially recruit new engram units rather than overwriting existing ones.

Because reactivation strength and behaviorally measured memory strength correlate in biological engrams, classification confidence can be read directly from the degree of engram reactivation rather than from an added readout layer.
This design yields falsifiable predictions.
It predicts that novel, high-error categories should recruit previously low-excitability, unallocated units rather than degrading existing class representations, mirroring competitive allocation.

It predicts that errors on ambiguous inputs should correspond to partial attractor convergence or silent engram-like states that are reactivatable but not spontaneously retrieved, paralleling silent engrams observed in amnesia research.

Remaining gaps include the absence of direct experimental tests of this exact combined circuit, uncertainty about how one neuromodulatory channel could carry class-specific teaching signals for many categories, and untested scalability of the sparse attractor-plus-predictive-coding scheme to deep hierarchies.
